reason: Attacked and held. I downloaded the full Gutenberg ebook 21774 (E. P. Dutton printing of Practical Mysticism: A Little Book for Normal People) and read it. The chapter heading WHAT IS MYSTICISM? stands at line 229. At line 271, set in italic (underscores in the transcription) and introduced at line 269 by the words 'Here is the definition:--', the text reads: '_Mysticism is the art of union with Reality. The mystic is a person who has attained that union in greater or less degree; or who aims at and believes in such attainment_.' The proposed quotation is the first sentence of that displayed definition, verbatim, with Reality capitalised, ending in a full stop, and the next sentence of the book is indeed 'It is not expected that the inquirer will find great comfort in this sentence when first it meets his eye.' Underhill quotes her own definition back at line 382 and again at line 3400, so it is the sentence the book is known by: the fame signal holds. shipped.js returns no match, no near match, Underhill at 0 of 3, not banned. Attribution is not in the misattribution list and is not disputed anywhere. In scope: a named prose work of 1914, not scripture or liturgy (Underhill is writing about mysticism as an art and cites Whitman and the philosophers, not a sacred text), nothing needing a content warning. Source line leads with the name, has no dash, uses curly quotes, and is 99 characters. Tag Philosophy is defensible for a ten-chapter treatise, although Underhill herself calls it 'this little essay' at line 260, so Essay would also be honest and would help the lane's Essay floor: that is an editor's choice, not a defect. Dutton & Company' (line 69), while the preface is dated September 12, 1914 (line 223). The 1914 in the source is the first publication (J. M. Dent and Sons, London); I did not open a Dent copy, so the wording is verified in the Dutton setting only. Same text, different imprint, and no variant is known.
